title: Cycling lanes and the shops that hate them

turns.speaker: Tasha
turns.text: The high street lane goes in next month and about forty businesses have signed a letter against it.

turns.speaker: Iris
turns.text: They always do. And then the surveys afterwards find the traders overestimated how many customers arrive by car by roughly four times.

turns.speaker: Iris
turns.text: It's one of the most replicated findings in transport research. Shopkeepers think two thirds drive. It's usually closer to a sixth.

turns.speaker: Tasha
turns.text: Because the shopkeeper drives, and so do the ones they talk to.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: I'd still be careful with that. It holds for a city centre. A hardware shop selling bags of cement is a different business.

turns.speaker: Iris
turns.text: That's true, and the good schemes keep loading bays. The bad ones remove everything and call it pedestrianisation.

turns.speaker: Tasha
turns.text: What actually changes the numbers is whether the lane is any good. A painted line beside moving traffic doesn't get anyone new on a bike.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Which is most of what gets built.

turns.speaker: Iris
turns.text: It is, and then the low usage gets quoted as proof that nobody wants to cycle here.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Alright, but there's a reasonable objection about who this is for. It tends to arrive in the neighbourhoods that were already doing well.

turns.speaker: Iris
turns.text: That's the criticism I think actually lands. The outer estates get the traffic and the centre gets the lane.

turns.speaker: Tasha
turns.text: So build it there first and see if the argument survives.

points: Around forty businesses signed a letter opposing a new high street cycle lane.
Iris cites replicated research that traders overestimate the share of customers arriving by car, often thinking two thirds when it is nearer a sixth.
Greg qualifies this, noting it holds for city centres but not for businesses selling heavy goods, and good schemes retain loading bays.
Tasha argues quality decides usage: a painted line beside moving traffic attracts no new cyclists.
Low usage of poor lanes is then cited as proof of no demand.
Greg's strongest objection is distributional, since lanes tend to arrive in already prosperous areas while outer estates absorb the traffic.
